newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine economic data dispels gloom.
newsitem.headline: Philippine economic data dispels gloom.

text.p: Healthy economic indicators this week have allayed fears that the Philippine economy might be heading for trouble after five years of steady growth, analysts said on Tuesday.
Last week, confidence and money began to flee the country as the stock market was savaged by investors who saw disturbing similarities to Thailand's property and banking crisis.
But this week, the government announced inflation was below expectations and exports were continuing to rise. Investors, unable to resist a bargain, began snapping up shares again.

"Our fundamentals are still intact. The figures show that the perception of the Philippines becoming another Thailand is a misconception," Manuel Lim, an economist at ING Bank in Manila, told Reuters.
The National Statistics Office (NSO) earlier reported a 17.4 percent growth to $5.5 billion in merchandise export receipts for the first quarter of the year.
It also cheered investors with news that inflation last month was only 4.6 percent, down from 4.8 percent the previous month and below what many analysts had expected.

Along with the data came a resurgence in the share market. The Manila share index rose 1.47 percent on Tuesday after making its biggest jump in more than three years on Monday with a leap of more than five percent.
"We will come out stronger from this, just as we did when the stock market went down due to the Mexico crisis (in late 1994)," Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo said in a statement.
"Perhaps the biggest lesson of the stock market fall is to have faith in ourselves that we are no longer the sick man of Asia and can now survive any adversity."
ING's Lim said healthy economic growth in the Philippines and the United States, its biggest trading partner, would further boost export earnings in the near term.

"We have already attained a growth momentum that will give us high gross national product growth this year. This momentum was helped by the fact that the policies in the past two to three years were very much focused on market liberalisation."

Concerns surfaced in early April that the economic bubble was about to burst as investors worried about similarities between the Philippines and Thailand's problems, caused by tumbling property values and banks beset with bad loans.
Sentiment worsened after a series of unexciting corporate results later in the month.

Analysts put this week's recovery in share prices -- after falling almost 18 percent in April -- down to a perception that prices of top shares had fallen too far and that the inflation and exports data had helped turn the market around.
Emilio Neri, economist of the University of Asia and the Pacific, rejected comparisons with Thailand's economic woes and predicted three more years of growth for the Philippines.
But he said that widening trade and current account deficits could spoil the story.
"Unless we do something about the strong peso (to help exports), we might not be able to sustain the growth," he said.
The peso has been steady against the U.S. dollar in the past months, but some economists are still advocating a weaker peso to encourage exports.

President Fidel Ramos also reassured investors, saying: "Our policies and programmes of social and economic reforms have been so deeply implanted in our country and so widely accepted by our people that they will surely survive next year's election and endure for well beyond the end of this century."
